text:
When a vehicle rolls onto a suspension bridge, its weight merges with the massive dead weight of the roadway itself, creating a downward force that cannot drop straight into the water or canyon below. Instead, the bridge routes this load along a carefully balanced path of pulling and pushing until it safely reaches the earth. Beneath the pavement, a stiffened framework of steel girders or open trusses spreads the localized weight of traffic across a broader section of the deck, preventing the road from dipping sharply under individual wheels. This rigid structure transfers the downward force outward to the edges of the roadway, where rows of vertical steel ropes, called suspender cables, are securely fastened. As gravity pulls the deck down, it stretches these vertical suspenders tight, placing them under pure tension.

The suspenders pull straight downward on the sweeping main cables slung high overhead. Spun from thousands of tightly bundled steel wires, these main cables are flexible rather than rigid, so the evenly spaced downward tugs from the suspenders naturally pull them into a smooth parabolic curve. Much like a clothesline weighed down by heavy laundry, the main cables carry the entire weight of the deck through tension, converting the vertical load hanging beneath them into an immense diagonal pulling force that travels upward along their curved length toward the tops of the bridge’s tall towers.

High in the air, the main cables rest inside heavy, curved metal troughs called saddles, which sit squarely atop the towers. Here, a major portion of the load transforms from tension into compression. Because the cables drape downward on both sides of each saddle, their opposing horizontal pulls largely balance one another out, while their combined downward pull presses straight down onto the crown of the tower. Built from thick cellular steel or reinforced concrete, the towers act as colossal pillars under compression, channeling millions of pounds of vertical force straight down through their legs. Beneath the waterline, the towers rest on broad concrete piers sunk deep through soft mud and silt until they bear directly upon solid bedrock, allowing the earth to support the crushing vertical weight.

Yet the towers alone cannot keep the bridge standing. The heavy central span constantly tugs the tops of the towers inward toward the middle of the crossing. To keep the towers from bending and collapsing into the water, the main cables continue past the saddles, sloping steeply down toward the shorelines. Where they meet the land, the cables enter massive structures called anchorages, fanning out into hundreds of individual strands embedded deep inside giant blocks of concrete or wedged directly into coastal rock cliffs. These anchorages hold the ends of the cables fast, using either sheer dead weight and ground friction or the grip of natural stone to resist the relentless inward and upward pull. Through this continuous chain, every ounce of weight on the deck is lifted by tension, carried outward by sweeping steel cables, driven down through compressed towers into underwater bedrock, and locked firmly into the ground on either shore.
